games.title: Thunderbirds await return meeting with Huskies
paragraphs: UBC got 137 rushing yards and a touchdown from Marvyn Larozar in its last meeting with Saskatchewan. It still lost by ten, a reminder that a good ground game does not leave much margin against the Huskies.

Saskatchewan won 34–24, getting two rushing touchdowns from Aulain Penner and 295 passing yards from Anton Amundrud. UBC's Drew Viotto threw two touchdown passes but was also intercepted twice, giving the Thunderbirds a productive afternoon with too many opportunities left behind.

That is what makes Larozar's role in the return meeting more interesting than his yardage alone. If his running helps UBC keep drives alive and avoid depending on difficult passing situations, it can change more than the balance of the offence.

The Huskies have been comfortable scoring through both Amundrud and the ground game, averaging 40.6 points through five outings. UBC has shown it can put points up against them too. The rematch gives the Thunderbirds a chance to turn that competitive performance into a different result by letting fewer possessions end in Saskatchewan's favour.

games.title: Vert & Or seek turnaround against Redbirds
paragraphs: Sherbrooke's first meeting with McGill produced one point. Its next game produced 310 passing yards from Jeremy Fyfe and a six-point loss to Montréal, a much more encouraging version of an offence still searching for a win.

The return meeting with the Redbirds gives Sherbrooke a chance to show that the improvement can survive against a team that had previously shut it down. McGill won 34–1 in September, part of a three-game winning streak.

The Redbirds have been getting better returns from their own offensive work. Elliott Drapeau threw two touchdown passes and ran for another against Bishop's, helping McGill reach 47 points without asking the passing game to do everything.

Sherbrooke has averaged 16.4 points through five games, so Fyfe's yardage against Montréal was a useful step rather than a finished answer. He gave the Vert & Or enough movement to keep the game close. Against McGill, the next step is making that movement worth more than the single point the first meeting allowed.

games.title: X-Men, Huskies meet in AUS finale
paragraphs: StFX has been winning with a scoring pace Saint Mary's rarely allows an opponent to reach. Their late-season meeting will test which team's recent experience travels better into a more difficult game.

The X-Men have scored 124 points during a three-game winning streak. Against Mount Allison, Deion Blackwood threw two touchdown passes and Aiden Rossong ran for two more, giving StFX more than one way to keep the scoreboard moving.

Saint Mary's has been able to win without needing that sort of total. The Huskies have allowed only 12.2 points a game, letting Malcolm Bussey's running help control contests rather than chase opponents who are already out of reach.
Bussey rushed for 124 yards and a touchdown against Acadia. His work would become even more useful against StFX if it keeps Blackwood and Rossong waiting for their next possession.

The X-Men have been good defensively too, allowing 15.8 points a game. That leaves both offences facing a version of the opponent that their recent results have not often required them to outscore. StFX has the larger scoring totals; Saint Mary's has been making smaller ones enough.

games.title: Gaiters seek more offence in Stingers rematch
paragraphs: Concordia needed only ten points to beat Bishop's in September. The Gaiters will want their improved passing game to make that a much less comfortable target in the rematch.

The 10–5 loss was followed by a 47–27 defeat against McGill, but Mathieu Bellavance threw two touchdown passes without an interception in that later game. Bishop's finally had more offence to work with, even if its defence did not let those points change the result.
Concordia has also found receiving production without finding enough scoring around it. Ely Rivest had 117 yards and a touchdown against Laval, only for the Stingers to lose 48–15.

That leaves two 1–4 teams with something more useful to bring into the return meeting than the memory of a 15-point game. Bellavance has shown he can finish drives through the air; Rivest has shown he can find space against a stronger opponent.

For Bishop's, the first of those developments is particularly important. The Gaiters do not need to turn this into a high-scoring game to change the result. They do need to give Concordia more to worry about than whether ten points will again be enough.

games.title: Dinos look to answer Golden Bears in return game
paragraphs: Calgary and Alberta combined for 77 points in September, and the Dinos still ended up seven short. Since then, Calgary has shown it can win a much quieter game. Alberta has shown how quickly its own offence can become quiet for the wrong reason.

The Dinos beat Regina 14–13 after the 42–35 loss to the Golden Bears. David Jordan passed for 215 yards without an interception, giving Calgary enough offensive stability to let a low-scoring game stay manageable.
Alberta's next outing went the other way. Eli Hetlinger was intercepted twice in an 18–3 loss to Manitoba, a sharp drop from the offence that had just beaten Calgary.

That leaves the return meeting less straightforward than the first score suggests. The Golden Bears have already proved they can trade touchdowns with the Dinos, but Calgary has also found a way to win without needing 35 points.

If Jordan can keep the passing game as clean as it was against Regina, Alberta may have to do more than reproduce a few of September's big offensive moments. It will have to make its own possessions last longer than they did against Manitoba.

paragraphs: Guelph heads to Windsor on October 31, with both teams looking to pick up a conference win. Guelph is 4–4; Windsor is 6–2.

games.title: Carabins get another shot at Rouge et Or
paragraphs: Montréal had 34 points the last time it played Laval and still finished eight short. The return meeting gives the Carabins another chance to make a good offensive day count against the Rouge et Or.

The 42–34 loss came in a game that left little room for either side to waste a scoring opportunity. Laval has continued at that pace, most recently getting three touchdown catches from Olivier Cool in a 48–15 win over Concordia.

Montréal's next win was less comfortable and less spectacular. Merton Theagene rushed for 116 yards against Sherbrooke as the Carabins worked through a 23–17 game, finding a result without approaching their usual scoring total.

That offers Montréal a useful alternative to simply trying to beat Laval in another exchange of touchdowns. If Theagene can help the Carabins sustain possessions, Victor Charland and Cool get fewer opportunities to make the return game look like the first.

The season averages show how little separates the offences: 39 points for Laval and 38.8 for Montréal. The first meeting showed how expensive even one additional successful drive can become when both teams can keep scoring.

games.title: Mounties, Axemen renew matchup in Wolfville
paragraphs: Mount Allison found 30 points against Acadia in September. Neither team has made scoring look that easy very often since, giving the Axemen a clear place to start when they get the return game at home.

The Mounties won the opener between them 30–13, but have averaged only 15.4 points through five games. Acadia has been quieter still at 14.4, with both sides facing difficult stretches against Saint Mary's and StFX.

There has been receiving production to work with. Quinten George had 96 yards for Mount Allison against the X-Men, while Acadia's Jase LeBlanc finished with 104 yards and a touchdown against the Huskies. In both cases, those catches came without enough scoring elsewhere to keep the game close.

That is why the first meeting stands out. Mount Allison turned its opportunities into a total that its other recent opponents have not allowed it to repeat. Acadia now has to keep that from becoming the pattern between these two teams, while making LeBlanc's receiving part of a more productive offence of its own.

games.title: Rams, Bisons prepare for another close contest
paragraphs: Regina has been running well enough to keep games close. Manitoba's latest win showed what can happen when a productive ground game is paired with a cleaner passing afternoon.

Carter Ashman rushed for 110 yards in the Rams' 14–13 loss to Calgary, but Owen Sieben was intercepted three times. That left Regina with its third straight narrow defeat and another reason to wonder how much more it needed to get from a game still within reach.

The Bisons had a different experience against Alberta. Ishe Matanga rushed for 122 yards, while Cole Anseeuw threw a touchdown without an interception in an 18–3 win. Manitoba did not need a large passing total because its offence avoided asking the defence to rescue too many lost possessions.

That makes the matchup more than a comparison between Ashman and Matanga's rushing yards. Both have shown they can give their teams useful work on the ground. The difference will be how much of it survives the rest of the drive. Regina has been finding enough yards to stay close; Manitoba has a recent example of turning that kind of afternoon into a win.
